description: The First and Second Noble Truths: the nature and causes of suffering, tanha and the three poisons.
content_html:
The Four Noble Truths: An Overview

The Buddha’s first formal teaching, recorded in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11), presented the Four Noble Truths as the framework for understanding and escaping suffering. These truths work like a medical diagnosis: the first identifies the illness, the second finds its cause, the third declares that a cure exists, and the fourth prescribes the treatment. This lesson examines the first two truths in detail.

The First Noble Truth: The Nature of Suffering (Dukkha)

The First Noble Truth (dukkha sacca) states that life is fundamentally characterised by dukkha. This does not mean that life is only pain, but that even the good things in life are shot through with unsatisfactoriness because they are impermanent. The Buddha identified three distinct types of suffering.

Key Fact

The three types of suffering are: Dukkha-dukkha (obvious physical and mental pain), Viparinama-dukkha (the suffering caused by things changing), and Sankhara-dukkha (the all-pervasive, existential suffering underlying all conditioned experience). The Dhammapada (verses 334–336) warns that craving is like a spreading creeper that overgrows those who do not cut it away.

Dukkha-dukkha is the most obvious kind of suffering. It covers straightforward physical pain—illness, injury, the discomfort of hunger or cold—and mental pain such as grief, fear, anxiety and depression. This is what most people mean when they use the word ‘suffering’, and it is universal: no human being escapes it.

Viparinama-dukkha is subtler. It is the suffering that comes from change. Even pleasant experiences carry a shadow because we know they will end. The happiness of a satisfying meal, a warm friendship, or a beautiful sunset is tinged with the awareness that it cannot last. When these things change or disappear, dissatisfaction follows. This type of suffering is closely related to the Mark of Existence known as anicca (impermanence).

Sankhara-dukkha is the deepest and most philosophically significant type. It refers to the background unsatisfactoriness that pervades all conditioned existence, even when we are not in obvious pain and things are not obviously changing. Simply existing as a conditioned being—subject to ignorance, craving and impermanence—means that existence itself is shot through with a subtle dis-ease. This type of suffering only becomes apparent through careful meditation and reflection.

A common misconception is that Buddhism is deeply pessimistic because it begins with the claim that life is suffering. However, Buddhist teachers are careful to point out that the First Noble Truth is not a claim that life contains nothing good, but rather an honest and clear-eyed acknowledgement of reality as it is. The word ‘dukkha’ is sometimes compared to a wheel with a slightly off-centre axle: most of the time the wheel turns smoothly, but there is always an underlying jolt. Recognising this is the first step toward freedom, not despair. Without an honest diagnosis, no cure is possible. The existence of the Third and Fourth Noble Truths means that Buddhism is ultimately an optimistic tradition: liberation is achievable.

The Second Noble Truth: The Cause of Suffering (Samudaya)

The Second Noble Truth (samudaya sacca) identifies the origin or cause of dukkha. The Pali word samudaya means ‘arising’ or ‘origin’. The Buddha taught that suffering arises from tanha—literally ‘thirst’ or ‘craving’. This craving takes three forms: craving for sensory pleasure (kama-tanha), craving for continued existence or becoming (bhava-tanha), and craving for non-existence or annihilation (vibhava-tanha). Each form of tanha keeps beings locked into the cycle of samsara.

Tanha is not simply ordinary desire or preference—everyone wants food when hungry or rest when tired, and these are natural. Tanha refers specifically to compulsive, grasping desire that arises from delusion: the mistaken belief that getting what we want (or avoiding what we dislike) will provide lasting satisfaction. Because all conditioned things are impermanent (anicca), no amount of getting what we crave can ever finally satisfy us. The craving simply generates more craving.

Key Fact

The three forms of tanha are craving for sensory pleasure (kama-tanha), craving for continued existence (bhava-tanha), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-tanha). All three forms keep beings trapped in the cycle of samsara according to the Second Noble Truth.

The Three Poisons (Three Fires)

Underlying tanha are the three poisons (also called the three fires or three roots). These are:
• Lobha (attachment or greed)—the grasping, possessive desire for pleasant things, pleasure and self-enhancement.
• Dosa (aversion, hatred or aggression)—the pushing away, rejection or hostility toward unpleasant things or people.
• Moha (ignorance or delusion)—the fundamental misunderstanding of reality, including the mistaken belief in a permanent self and the impermanent things can bring lasting happiness.

The three poisons are depicted at the hub of the Tibetan Wheel of Life as a pig (Moha), a snake (Dosa) and a bird (Lobha), each biting the tail of the next. This image powerfully conveys how the three poisons fuel one another and keep the wheel of samsara spinning. Moha is considered the most fundamental poison because Lobha and Dosa both arise from the ignorant misperception of self and world. The Dhammapada (verses 334–336) uses the image of a creeping vine to warn that craving, if not cut away, will overgrow a person like weeds smothering a garden.

Different Buddhist schools interpret the three poisons with different nuances. In Theravada teaching, Moha (ignorance) specifically refers to not understanding the Four Noble Truths and the Three Marks of Existence. Lobha is understood as sensory passion and attachment. Dosa is anger, ill-will and hatred.

In some Mahayana interpretations, ignorance (sometimes called avidya) is understood more broadly as the fundamental misperception of all phenomena—not just the self—as having inherent, independent existence (related to sunyata, or emptiness). Aversion can also be understood more subtly as any form of rejection or resistance, not just obvious anger. What all traditions agree on is that these three roots generate all unskilful action and, through the law of kamma, generate the suffering that follows from it. Removing the three poisons is therefore central to the Buddhist path.
exam_tip_html: A very common student error is to say that the Second Noble Truth teaches that ‘desire is the cause of suffering’ without distinguishing between ordinary preference and compulsive tanha (craving). Examiners expect precision: make clear that tanha is grasping, compulsive desire fuelled by the three poisons, not simply wanting things. For ‘Outline’ questions on the three types of dukkha, name each type with its Pali term and give a one-sentence explanation. The 15-mark ‘Discuss’ question will reward accurate spelling of technical terms such as ‘Dukkha-dukkha’, ‘Viparinama-dukkha’, ‘Samudaya’, ‘Tanha’, ‘Lobha’, ‘Dosa’ and ‘Moha’. When you ‘Explain’ the Second Noble Truth, always connect it to how tanha arises from the three poisons—this shows the deeper level of understanding that earns top marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The First Noble Truth (Dukkha) identifies three types of suffering: Dukkha-dukkha (physical/mental pain), Viparinama-dukkha (suffering from change) and Sankhara-dukkha (all-pervasive existential unsatisfactoriness).
  • The Second Noble Truth (Samudaya) identifies tanha (craving) as the cause of suffering; tanha takes three forms: craving for sensory pleasure, craving for existence and craving for non-existence.
  • Tanha is fuelled by the three poisons: Lobha (attachment/greed), Dosa (aversion/hatred) and Moha (ignorance/delusion); Moha is the most fundamental, as it underlies the other two.

practice_questions.text: State the Pali term for the Second Noble Truth about the cause of suffering.
practice_questions.marks: Samudaya (also accept tanha as the named cause, or 'the arising of suffering'). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Buddhists mean by tanha.
practice_questions.marks: Tanha means craving or thirst; it is compulsive, grasping desire—not ordinary preference—that arises from delusion about what can bring lasting satisfaction. 1 mark: identifying tanha as craving/desire. 2 marks: explaining that it is compulsive/grasping and identified as the cause of suffering. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the three types of suffering described in the First Noble Truth.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per type of suffering, each requiring the Pali term and a brief explanation:
• Dukkha-dukkha—obvious physical and mental pain such as illness, injury and grief.
• Viparinama-dukkha—the suffering that arises when pleasant things change or end.
• Sankhara-dukkha—the deep, all-pervasive unsatisfactoriness of all conditioned existence. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the role of the three poisons in causing suffering according to Buddhist teaching.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The three poisons are Lobha (attachment/greed), Dosa (aversion/hatred) and Moha (ignorance/delusion). They are the root causes of tanha and therefore of all suffering.
• Moha is the most fundamental poison because it is ignorance of the true nature of reality (impermanence, no-self) that gives rise to both Lobha and Dosa.
• When we wrongly believe things can give permanent satisfaction, Lobha arises; when we wrongly believe things can be permanent threats, Dosa arises.
• The Tibetan Wheel of Life depicts the three poisons as a pig, snake and bird at the hub, showing how they fuel the cycle of samsara.
• The Dhammapada (334–336) warns that craving, if not eliminated, will overgrow the person.
• Removing the three poisons through the Eightfold Path is what ends suffering.
Mastering: all three poisons explained with their role in generating tanha, named references used, clear causal chain shown.
Secure: two or three poisons explained with a named reference and development.
Developing: basic description of the three poisons with limited explanation of how they cause suffering.
Emerging: names one or two poisons without explanation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The most important of the three poisons is Moha (ignorance).'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Moha is the foundational poison: both Lobha (greed) and Dosa (hatred) are said to arise from ignorance about the true nature of reality—specifically, the mistaken belief in a permanent self and in things that can provide lasting satisfaction.
• If Moha were removed, Lobha and Dosa would have no ground in which to grow. Eliminating ignorance is therefore the most direct path to ending all suffering.
• Buddhist practice—especially meditation and the cultivation of wisdom (panna)—specifically targets ignorance, suggesting the tradition itself views Moha as the primary problem.
• The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11) places ignorance at the start of the chain of dependent origination, confirming its priority.

Arguments against or offering a different emphasis:
• In practice, many Buddhists find Lobha (craving/attachment) the most destructive poison in daily life; attachment to people, pleasure and possessions causes obvious suffering and is the everyday form of tanha.
• Dosa (hatred and aversion) leads to harmful actions that damage individuals and communities; some might argue that reducing hatred has the most immediate beneficial impact.
• Theravada teaching describes Moha, Lobha and Dosa as interdependent—they constantly reinforce one another, so prioritising one over the others may be misleading.
• The Dhammapada (334–336) focuses specifically on craving (Lobha/tanha) as the creeper that overgrows the person, suggesting the tradition sometimes foregrounds attachment rather than ignorance.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammapada 334–336), explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with at least one named reference and a clear conclusion.
Developing: some argument on each side with limited sources and a weak conclusion.
Emerging: one-sided response with no sources. [15 marks, SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the three types of tanha identified in the Second Noble Truth.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per type of tanha, each requiring identification and a brief explanation:
• Kama-tanha—craving for sensory pleasure; the desire for pleasant sensory experiences.
• Bhava-tanha—craving for continued existence or becoming; the desire for rebirth or for things to continue.
• Vibhava-tanha—craving for non-existence or annihilation; the desire to escape existence entirely rather than following the Buddhist path. [3 marks]

flashcard_questions.q: What Pali term names the First Noble Truth about suffering?

flashcard_questions.a: Suffering caused when pleasant things change or come to an end.
The deep, all-pervasive unsatisfactoriness underlying all conditioned existence.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Second Noble Truth identify as the cause of suffering?
flashcard_questions.a: Tanha — craving or thirst, particularly compulsive grasping desire.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three forms of tanha?
flashcard_questions.a: Kama-tanha (sensory craving), Bhava-tanha (craving for existence), Vibhava-tanha (craving for non-existence).

flashcard_questions.q: What sutta first sets out the First and Second Noble Truths?
What does the Dhammapada (334–336) compare craving to?
flashcard_questions.a: A spreading creeper that overgrows those who fail to cut it away.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three poisons in Buddhism?
What is Moha and why is it considered the most fundamental poison?
flashcard_questions.a: Ignorance or delusion; it is the root from which Lobha and Dosa both arise.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Tibetan Wheel of Life depict the three poisons?
flashcard_questions.a: As a pig (Moha), snake (Dosa) and bird (Lobha) at the hub, each biting the next's tail.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the First Noble Truth not considered pessimistic by Buddhists?
flashcard_questions.a: Because honestly recognising suffering is the necessary first step toward the cure—liberation is possible.

glossary_terms.definition: The Buddha's first discourse after his Enlightenment, delivered at Sarnath, in which he set out the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
The First Noble Truth: that life is characterised by suffering, unsatisfactoriness and imperfection.
Suffering, unsatisfactoriness and imperfection; the First Noble Truth and also one of the Three Marks of Existence.
The first type of suffering: obvious physical and mental pain, such as illness, injury, grief and fear.
The second type of suffering: the unhappiness that comes when pleasant things change or end.
The third type of suffering: the deep, all-pervasive unsatisfactoriness underlying all conditioned existence, even in neutral moments.
The Second Noble Truth: that the cause of suffering is craving, clinging and unsatisfied desire (tanha).
The Sanskrit/Pali term for 'arising' or 'origin'; identifies the cause of suffering as tanha in the Second Noble Truth.
Craving or thirst; the clinging desire for sensory pleasure, for continued existence, or for non-existence, that is identified as the cause of suffering.
The three root causes of all unwholesome action and suffering in Buddhism: Lobha (attachment/greed), Dosa (aversion/hatred) and Moha (ignorance/delusion).
Greed, attachment or passion; one of the three poisons that fuels craving and suffering.
Aversion, hatred or aggression; one of the three poisons that drives the rejection of what is unpleasant.
Ignorance or delusion; the most fundamental of the three poisons, from which Lobha and Dosa arise.
